sections.title: About you
sections.description: Your identity, relationship, children and anything that complicates the picture.
sections.intro: Your legal identity, exactly as it should appear on your will.

questions.label: Full legal name
questions.help: As shown on your passport or driver licence.
questions.why: Your will must name you precisely, or assets held in another name can be disputed later.

questions.label: Any other names you've used (aliases)
questions.help: Maiden names or former names your assets may be held under.
questions.why: If your home or super is in an old name, your lawyer will note both so nothing gets stuck.

questions.label: Date of birth
questions.why: In Queensland you generally must be 18 or older. Your age also helps your lawyer spot issues like capacity checks for older will-makers.

questions.label: Do you live in Queensland?
questions.why: This service prepares wills under Queensland law. Living elsewhere doesn't stop you, but your lawyer may need extra care with interstate or overseas property.

questions.label: Residential address
questions.why: Your address appears in the will's opening declaration to identify you.

questions.label: Occupation
questions.why: Traditional wills describe the will-maker by name, address and occupation — it helps prove identity.

questions.label: Mobile number
questions.why: Your lawyer may call with questions instead of making you wait for an appointment.

questions.label: What is your current relationship status?
questions.why: Marriage can revoke an existing will in Queensland, and an ex-spouse may still have claims. Your lawyer checks this carefully.

questions.label: Partner's full legal name
questions.why: So your will can name your partner exactly — especially important if they're your executor or a beneficiary.

questions.label: Partner's date of birth
questions.why: Helps your lawyer identify the right person unambiguously.

questions.label: Did you marry or partner recently, or plan to soon?
questions.why: In Queensland, marrying generally cancels a will made before the marriage. Your lawyer will confirm the advice that applies to you.

questions.label: Are formal proceedings or a property settlement complete?
questions.why: Until a settlement is final, your former spouse may still be entitled to claim.

questions.label: Are you planning to marry or enter a civil partnership soon?
questions.why: A will is generally revoked by marriage unless it's written in contemplation of that marriage — your lawyer can add the right words.

questions.label: Do you have any children — including adopted, step, or from earlier relationships?
questions.why: Children — including step-children you treat as your own — can have legal claims on your estate whether or not they're in the will.

questions.label: Your children
questions.why: Ages, relationships and any special circumstances guide guardianship, trust provisions, and risk of a family provision claim.

fields.label: This child is from a previous relationship
This child has a disability or special needs
Include this child in my will

questions.label: Do you already have a will anywhere?
questions.why: Most wills start by revoking earlier ones. An overseas will may need to stay in place for overseas assets.

questions.label: Do you want this will to revoke it?
questions.why: Keeping two wills can work for assets in different countries, but done wrong it can cancel parts you meant to keep.

questions.label: Is any existing will made overseas?
questions.why: Revoking an overseas will by accident can leave foreign assets without instructions.

questions.label: Do you own or control any of these?
questions.why: These don't always pass under a will — they need specific planning, and your lawyer is flagged to review them.

questions.label: Is someone helping you complete this questionnaire?
questions.help: Help is completely fine — we just need to know who.
questions.why: A will must be your own free decision. If the person helping also benefits from your will, we pause and speak with you privately. It protects your will from being challenged later.

questions.label: Who is helping you?
questions.why: So your lawyer knows who was present — it's recorded on the file, nothing more.

questions.label: Does that person receive anything under your will?
questions.why: If so, we'll arrange a short private conversation with you before going further — standard practice that makes your will much harder to challenge.

questions.label: Does anyone else rely on you financially? (other than children)
questions.help: For example, a parent you support or a grandchild in your care.
questions.why: Dependants may have claims on your estate even if you leave them nothing.

questions.label: Who depends on you, and how?
questions.why: A short note now lets your lawyer plan properly rather than discovering it later.

sections.title: Guardians
sections.description: Who raises your children if you can't — and what happens to money meant for them.
sections.intro: Because you have children under 18, you can nominate who should care for them.

questions.label: Do you want to appoint a testamentary guardian?
questions.help: Any surviving parent with parental responsibility usually continues regardless.
questions.why: Naming a guardian puts your wishes on the record. Courts still decide on the child's best interests, but your nomination carries real weight.

questions.label: Guardian — full name
questions.why: A full legal name avoids confusion with relatives of the same first name.

questions.label: Their relationship to you
questions.why: Context for your lawyer and, if ever needed, for a court.

questions.label: Guardian's address
questions.why: So the right person can be identified and found.

questions.label: Backup guardian — full name (optional)
questions.why: If your first choice can't act, a written backup saves the family a difficult decision.

questions.label: Backup guardian's address (optional)
questions.why: One plain-text line is enough for a backup.

questions.label: Same guardian for all your children?
questions.why: Splitting siblings is unusual and emotional; your lawyer will want to understand the reasoning.

questions.label: Which children, and who? (explain)
questions.why: Your lawyer drafts the appointment per child from this note.

questions.label: Do the children's other parent(s) live and have parental responsibility?

options.label: Yes — living with full parental responsibility
Yes — but orders limit their role

questions.why: A surviving parent with parental responsibility normally decides, whatever the will says. Conflict here means your lawyer must advise before approval.

questions.label: Any wishes about upbringing? (optional — schooling, faith, sport, contact)
questions.why: Not legally binding, but guardians genuinely read and follow these wishes.

questions.label: Do you want money held for the children until a certain age?
questions.why: A trust until 21–30 protects young people from inheriting too young, and adds tax advantages. Choosing one flags your matter for extra lawyer review.

sections.title: Pets
sections.description: Who feeds the dog — and whether money follows.
sections.intro: Answer no and this step quietly skips itself.

questions.label: Do you have pets that will need care?
questions.why: Pets are property at law — without a direction, they can end up anywhere.

questions.label: Your pets
questions.why: Names and types make the direction unambiguous.

questions.label: Do you want to leave money for their care?
questions.why: A modest sum with the right person is enforceable; a fortune for a cat invites a court challenge.

questions.label: Amount for pet care
questions.why: Over $20,000 flags a lawyer review — large gifts to pets get contested more than almost anything.

questions.label: Care instructions (optional — vet, diet, quirks)
questions.why: The carer gets this note with the will. Small compassions.

sections.title: Executors
sections.description: The people who carry out your wishes — and the backups behind them.
sections.intro: Your executor is the person who actually does the work after you die: finding assets, paying debts, and giving people what you left them. Choose someone organised, trustworthy and likely to outlive you.

questions.label: Your executor(s) — up to 4
questions.why: You can appoint up to four people to act together. Two is common: it shares the load and covers illness or travel.

fields.label: I confirm this person is 18 or older

questions.label: Do you want substitute executor(s), in case your first choice cannot act?
questions.why: Executors die, move overseas and fall ill. A substitute keeps the will working without a court application.

questions.label: Substitute executor(s)
questions.why: They only step in if your first choice can't or won't act.

questions.label: Is any executor also a major beneficiary of your will?
questions.help: This is completely normal — most people appoint their partner or adult child.
questions.why: It's allowed and common in Queensland. We ask so your lawyer can make sure the will is worded to avoid any suggestion of conflict.

questions.label: Does any executor you've named fit one of these? (tick all that apply)

options.label: Is bankrupt or has been recently
Has difficulty managing their own affairs

questions.why: An executor under 18 cannot act — we'll stop and ask you to choose someone else. Overseas or bankrupt executors are allowed but create real practical problems, so your lawyer will talk them through with you.

questions.label: Would you like a professional executor instead, or alongside?
questions.help: Professional executors charge fees from the estate, typically a percentage.
questions.why: Useful for complex estates or when family conflict is likely. If you're interested, your lawyer will send you a written quote before anything is finalised.

questions.label: Have you actually spoken to the people you've named?
questions.why: Nobody is forced to be an executor — they can refuse after you die, which causes delay. A quick conversation now prevents that.

sections.title: Divide your estate
sections.description: Everything left after gifts and debts — who receives it, and what happens if they don't.
sections.intro: Your 'residuary estate' is everything left after debts, funeral costs and any specific gifts are paid out. For most people it's the biggest part of the will — the family home, super, savings.

questions.label: Which of these do you own?
questions.why: Some assets — super, jointly-owned homes, trust assets — don't automatically follow your will. This list tells your lawyer where to look.

questions.label: Roughly, what is everything worth, before debts?
questions.why: Scale changes advice: bigger estates trigger senior review and sometimes tax structuring. Estimates are completely fine.

questions.label: Have you made a binding death benefit nomination with your super fund?
questions.why: A binding nomination can override your will for that money. 'Not sure' is fine — your lawyer will tell you how to check.

questions.label: If you own property, how is it held?
questions.help: Joint tenants: the survivor automatically gets the whole thing. Tenants in common: your share passes under your will.
questions.why: This single answer decides whether your home passes under your will at all. If you're unsure, your lawyer can check the title.

questions.label: Any significant debts or mortgages we should know about? (optional)
questions.placeholder: e.g. mortgage on Ashgrove property, personal loan
questions.why: Debts are paid before anyone inherits. Knowing them stops a gift being wiped out unexpectedly.

questions.label: How would you like to divide your residuary estate?

options.label: Split among named people and charities

questions.why: Most wills use one of the first two. The named option lets you set exact percentages with the slider tool.

questions.label: Your partner's full name
questions.why: Named exactly as elsewhere in the will — variations create doubt.

questions.label: If they die before you, who then?
questions.placeholder: e.g. my children in equal shares
questions.why: A backup stops this part of the will failing if the unthinkable happens twice.

questions.label: Who receives your residuary estate? (shares must total 100%)
questions.why: Shares must total exactly 100% or the will is ambiguous — the slider tool won't let you get it wrong.

fields.label: Charity ABN (look up)
fields.placeholder: Search a charity name or ABN

questions.label: Describe how you'd like it divided
questions.why: Your lawyer will draft this properly and confirm the wording with you before approval.

questions.label: If a beneficiary dies before you, what should happen to their share?

options.label: Share it among the surviving beneficiaries

questions.help: 'Their children take their share' is the most common choice for family wills.
questions.why: Without this rule, a share can fail entirely and fall into intestacy — the law's default, not yours.

questions.label: Describe what should happen instead
questions.why: Custom survivorship rules need careful drafting — your lawyer reviews this one closely.

questions.label: If everyone named dies before you, who should inherit?
questions.placeholder: e.g. my cousins equally, or RSPCA Queensland
questions.help: This 'ultimate default' prevents your estate passing under government intestacy rules.
questions.why: It almost never happens — but without this line, your estate can end up with the state.

questions.label: Is any beneficiary under 18, living with a disability, or receiving government benefits?
questions.why: A direct inheritance can cut someone off a pension or NDIS support. A protective trust usually fixes this — your lawyer will advise.

questions.label: Is there anyone who might expect to benefit that you're choosing not to provide for?
questions.help: A spouse, child, step-child or dependant. There's no judgement here — people have good reasons.
questions.why: In Queensland these people can apply to a court for provision from your estate. Saying so now lets your lawyer protect your wishes properly.

questions.label: Who are you choosing not to provide for?
questions.why: Names, exact — same reason.

questions.label: Your reasons (kept confidential with your lawyer)
questions.help: Be factual rather than emotional — it carries more weight.
questions.why: A calm, factual statement recorded now can defeat a claim years later. A lawyer will talk this through with you before anything is finalised.

sections.title: Specific gifts
sections.description: Particular things or amounts you want to go to particular people.
sections.intro: Gifts are handed out before the rest of your estate is divided. Say no and this step skips itself.

questions.label: Do you want to leave any specific gifts?
questions.help: For example: $5,000 to a grandchild, your wedding ring to a niece, or your car to a friend.
questions.why: Specific gifts come out first, so they need exact wording to survive the years between writing and reading.

questions.label: Your gifts
questions.why: Clarity here prevents two people claiming the same ring.

options.label: It falls into my residuary estate
It goes to a named backup person

fields.label: Backup recipient
fields.placeholder: Only if you chose a named backup

fields.label: A short message with this gift (optional)

questions.label: Do you hold significant digital assets generally?
questions.help: Cryptocurrency, online businesses, monetised channels, or large photo libraries.
questions.why: If nobody can find your accounts, they may as well not exist. Your executor needs a direction and a way to access keys.

sections.title: Funeral wishes
sections.description: How you'd like to be farewelled — plus your final declarations.
sections.intro: Funerals happen quickly, often before anyone reads the will. Writing this down takes the weight off your family at the worst possible moment.

questions.label: Burial, cremation, or no preference?

options.label: No preference — let my family decide

questions.why: This is the single question families most often wish had been answered.

questions.label: Preferred location (optional)
questions.placeholder: e.g. Toowong Cemetery family plot, or scattered at Manly
questions.why: Specific places matter to people. Writing it down removes the guesswork.

questions.label: What kind of service?
questions.why: Families often disagree about this. Your written wish usually settles it.

questions.label: Music you'd like (optional)
questions.why: A small kindness to the person planning the day.

questions.label: Readings, poems or speakers (optional)
questions.why: Same reason — it gives your family something to hold onto.

questions.label: Flowers or donations?
questions.why: Charities receive a great deal through 'in lieu of flowers' requests.

questions.label: Which charity should donations go to?
questions.why: Naming it means your family doesn't have to choose for you.

questions.label: Your organ and tissue donation wishes

options.label: Yes — I want to be a donor

questions.help: Important: a will is usually read days after a donation decision must be made, so this is a record of your wishes — not a legally binding direction.
questions.why: Register your decision on the Australian Organ Donor Register as well — and tell your family, because they're asked to confirm it.

questions.label: Do you have a prepaid funeral or funeral bond?
questions.why: Families routinely pay twice because nobody knew a plan existed.

questions.label: Provider name
questions.why: So your executor can find and use it.

questions.label: Policy or contract number
questions.why: Saves your executor an afternoon on the phone.

questions.label: Who should be told first?
questions.why: One calm person to make the first calls. It's often not the executor.

questions.label: Their phone number
questions.why: So whoever finds this document can reach them immediately.

questions.label: A personal message to the people you love (optional)
questions.placeholder: Anything you'd like them to read.
questions.why: Not legally operative — but for many families, the part of the will they keep.

questions.label: I declare the information provided is true and complete to the best of my knowledge.
questions.why: Your lawyer relies on what you tell them — the will is only as good as its inputs.

questions.label: I understand the nature and effect of making a will, and no one is pressuring me to make it.
questions.why: Capacity and freedom from pressure are what make a will legally valid.

questions.label: I understand this questionnaire is not legal advice, and a lawyer will review my answers before any will is issued.
questions.why: This is how the service keeps its promise: software collects, a human solicitor checks.
